label: abstract; sec:phil:craig (paragraph after rem:phil:craig); phil.tex l.55; discussion 'What the formalism shows'
problem: Exhaustive upshot 'where shape matters, it is relative to a reasoner and a vocabulary, and only when the written theory is charged' goes beyond what is proved: separations are proved only in shape's model (also under the time-charged inducer Kt) and in terms' settings (charged derivations, finite theories); synthesis §2.8 row 2 marks the extension open; the 'only when the written theory is charged' is contradicted by §7 (time) and §8 (derivations).
fix: Scope every occurrence to 'in the settings we study': shape becomes visible only when something other than program length is charged (written length, running time or derivations) or the hypothesis class is restricted; say the extension beyond these models is open (q:shape:beyond). Abstract: 'in the settings where we find that shape matters, it matters relative to a reasoner and a vocabulary'.

label: sec:phil:craig (paragraph after rem:phil:craig); discussion 'What the formalism shows'
problem: 'We still find it plausible that good theories are shaped like logical theories' is asserted without grounds, is endorsed by neither the philosophy record nor the synthesis, and sits against the paper's own findings (logical form as such buys at most a constant factor in the only formal model; 'declarative is not sentential').
fix: Replace by: 'We accept the observation that written theories are declarative, and think it likely that this shape is good for reasons our formalism does not model, such as communication, division of labour and piecemeal checking (q:phil:declarative); but in the only formal model we have, logical form as such buys at most a constant factor, and nothing in our results favours sentences over classes of models.' Same change in the discussion.

label: sec:phil:observation ('Declarative is not sentential'); sec:kepler:pool (paragraph after 'What the data decide and what the syntax decides')
problem: The semantic-view objection (the language relativity of §10 is an artefact of a prior on texts) is not answered; the record's answer is dropped: the Kepler computation is mostly semantic (compatibility = region of element space, Occam factor = its measure), a presentation-free prior selects the ellipse at every delta<=60' by small, parametrisation-dependent margins, and the rejoinder (a prior over infinitely many model families needs an enumeration, i.e. a presentation; volume priors depend on parametrisation) relocates rather than removes the relativity. Halvorson and Lutz appear only in a background list.
fix: Add three sentences after 'relative to the language of the law texts' in kepler.tex (or a paragraph 'The semantic view' in sec:phil:observation): the computation is mostly semantic; only the law-text prior is syntactic; with a presentation-free prior the data alone select the ellipse at every delta<=60' (margins 0.20-14.61 bits, parametrisation-dependent at the one-bit level); but a prior over infinitely many families needs a presentation and volume priors depend on the parametrisation, so the relativity is relocated, not removed. Cite halvorson2012what, lutz2017what where the semantic view is introduced.

label: sec:intro:contrib item (10) (and laws.tex prop:laws:kink title)
problem: 'Lewis's kind nature is a kink' overstates the match: the proposition shows robustness of the best system to the balance lambda with the measures of simplicity and fit fixed; Lewis's kindness answers the worry that the standards of simplicity and strength and balance come from us, i.e. includes robustness to the simplicity standard, which is the language relativity §10 shows can fail; the one Lewis sentence seen ('how kind nature is') is about how good the best balance is.
fix: Intro (10): 'the best system is the same for every balance of simplicity against strength in an interval exactly when the hull of length against fit has a kink there, which formalises one aspect of what Lewis calls a kind nature (robustness to the balance, with the measures of simplicity and fit fixed)'. Suggest retitling prop:laws:kink 'Robustness to the balance is a kink' and adding that robustness to the simplicity standard is the language relativity of §10. Check Lewis 1994 wording against the text before quoting.

label: related 'Universal and operator induction'; sec:phil:differences; sec:limits:other
problem: SAI is Bayesian confirmation theory with a universal prior and 0/1 (hypothetico-deductive) likelihoods, but the paper never positions it against that literature's standard problems (priors/language dependence and grue; tacking; Carnap's zero probability for laws, which SAI avoids; the catch-all, which universality removes at the price of incomputability); only Duhem and old evidence appear. 'Nothing here depends on' the justification of simplicity is too strong: the use of SAI as an ideal of evaluation does.
fix: Replace 'nothing here depends on it' by 'our theorems do not depend on it; our use of SAI as an ideal of evaluation does, and we take the universal prior as a modelling choice whose machine dependence is bounded by the invariance theorem but, at the scale of our examples, not negligible'. Add a short paragraph 'SAI as Bayesian confirmation' in §6 covering (a)-(e) with pointers (thm:basic:translation, prop:logic:omega, prop:logic:oldevidence, Table 2 items 5, 7, 11); cite carnap1950logical; add Goodman/Earman/Howson-Urbach only after the bibliography editor verifies them. Add to §11 that verdicts are relative to the universal machine up to constants not small at the scale of real theories.

label: phil 'What rests on theorems'; sec:limits:approx; discussion 'What the formalism shows'
problem: 'Approximate truth is a limitation of proof-requiring compatibility with deterministic theories, not of the axiom view' overreads the theorems: the preferred hypothesis (law with calibrated error model) is a randomised theory whose error model lives in the machine's coin flips, not in any axiom (and by thm:soi:onetape is equally a random labeller); §11.1 itself says a native statistical treatment is open. The identification with 'the axiom view' is an assessment, listed in §6 under 'Proved'.
fix: Write 'not of SAI: its mixture contains randomised theories, and under its pricing an approximately true law is a law with a calibrated error model. The error model is carried by the randomness of the theory, not stated as an axiom, so for the axiom view in the narrow sense approximate truth remains tied to the statistical limitation of §11.1.' Move the reading to the arguments list in 'What rests on theorems'.

label: abstract upshot; intro 'What a theory is'; rem:phil:craig; tab:phil:differences items 2, 4; discussion
problem: The headline 'the idealised formalism cannot see the difference between a theory and a program' is stated without its scope (data labelled true/false; representation, vocabulary, reasoner, formulation, per synthesis §2.8), although prop:soi:independent proves an unbounded idealised separation of theories from labellers when 'independent' is observed (partiality: silent without committing), and prop:soi:closure a closure difference in the semimeasure convention; the paper files both under D (Table 2) though they compare theories with labellers (claim S). 'And this is a theorem' (intro) overstates: the neutrality reading is an assessment.
fix: Scope the headline to 'on data labelled true or false' in abstract, intro and §13; intro: 'this rests on theorems, and the reading is ours'. In sec:phil:craig add that the one respect in which the idealised formalism separates theories from labellers is partiality (prop:soi:independent; closure, prop:soi:closure), with data that arise in mathematics rather than observation and with no r.e. witnesses (prop:soi:noRE): a formal trace of the partiality candidate, not support for S in empirical science. Mark Table 2 items 2, 4 as comparisons with operator induction bearing on S.

label: intro 'Raw data and questions'; phil 'The ladder'
problem: The agreed stance requires saying plainly that steps 3 and 4 of the ladder are needed; the paper says only that step 2 is a step in the right direction and that it has partial results on step 3.
fix: Add 'but not the end point: an account of what theories do needs steps 3 and 4 as well' in the intro and in 'The ladder'.

label: intro first paragraph; sec:phil first paragraph
problem: The intro's composite 'second view' cites van Fraassen (a semantic-view proponent, for whom answering why-questions is a pragmatic use of a theory, not its aim) alongside the received view; Kuhn and Polanyi are glossed as holding that a theory is a practice of exemplars and skills.
fix: Separate: received view (Suppe) with answers derived from it; 'on van Fraassen's account, explanations are answers to why-questions'; 'or that scientific knowledge rests on exemplars and tacit skills (Kuhn; Polanyi)'.

label: sec:phil:questions, sentence before prop:phil:answers
problem: 'A raw-data predictor answers one question ... and answers it fully' is a strawman: a predictive measure assigns probabilities to every event about future observations; what it lacks is answers to non-observational questions (laws, unobservables) and a notion of leaving a question open.
fix: 'A raw-data predictor is scored on one question, what is the next observation?, and answers every question about future observations with a total distribution: it has no notion of a question left open, and answers questions about laws only as questions about all future data (Table 2 item 5).'

label: sec:phil:explanation
problem: The paper's own preferred approximate laws (laws with error models, prop:laws:errormodel) make data probable rather than derive them, so statistical explanation (Hempel's I-S case; Salmon's S-R model) is a further gap of 'explanation as derivation'; 'EP makes this precise' overstates (Kitcher's unification concerns argument patterns).
fix: 'gives one precise measure of this'; add the gap 'statistical explanation' citing salmon1971statistical (citable for the S-R model); update the count of gaps in §6 and Table 1 row E.

label: discussion 'What it cannot show' (also intro sec:intro:notclaim, end of sec:phil:craig)
problem: 'So it supports no realist conclusion' infers a blanket refusal from an adversarial possibility result and ignores the paper's own truth-tracking result (prop:basic:limits: complete truths presented by the data are identified).
fix: 'it supports no general realist conclusion: it identifies complete truths that the data present (prop:basic:limits), but its limit posterior can live on random theories and, with adversarially chosen true data, on false ones'.

label: sec:limits:domains
problem: 'Physicists rarely state or propagate tolerances' is too broad: measurement uncertainties are propagated routinely and effective theories estimate truncation errors.
fix: 'physicists rarely state or propagate worst-case bounds on the error of an approximate model (measurement uncertainties are propagated routinely, and statistically)'.

label: sec:limits:other ('The mathematics is free, and large')
problem: 'Charging for it changes little in the universal setting' overstates a bound of K(B')+c bits, a data-independent constant that is not small for the mathematics physics uses and matters when rival theories need different mathematics.
fix: 'gains at most K(B')+c bits on any data (prop:basic:background), a constant that does not grow with the data but is not small for the mathematics physics uses, and matters when rival theories need different mathematics'.

label: phil 'What rests on theorems' (Hempel item); related 'Craig, Ramsey, Hempel'
problem: 'Beyond a constant factor' is not given its operational meaning: a factor 2^{±2c} can flip any single prediction; the theorem bounds the total effect of theoretical vocabulary on cumulative log loss by a machine-dependent constant number of bits.
fix: Add '(theoretical vocabulary can change the cumulative loss over any data by at most a constant number of bits, which depends on the universal machine)' in §6 and 'that is, by a bounded number of bits over all data' in §12.

label: sec:phil:map, paragraph 'What rests on theorems'
problem: 'Answering questions differs from raw-data prediction in target, data type, coherence and partiality, not in the inference principle' is listed as proved; synthesis §2.8 row 5 says the reading is an assessment.
fix: Append '(the theorems proved; this reading of them an argument)'.

label: tab:phil:differences item 11
problem: Says 'the base language decides real choices, such as the preferred orbit of Mars'; in §10 the data language is fixed and only the primitives for writing laws (S1-S3) change; 'base language' is the ladder's term for the data/question language.
fix: 'within that bound the primitives in which laws are written decide real choices, such as the preferred orbit of Mars on noise-free interval data'.

label: sec:limits:concepts
problem: 'We accept them all as features of human concepts' drops the record's 'comparatively' for the first feature ('for questions and problems, not predictions'), which §6 defends only in comparative form.
fix: 'We accept them as features of human concepts, the first only comparatively (sec:phil:map), with two further qualifications: ...'.

label: related 'Learning theories from data'
problem: Shapiro's model inference is called the nearest precedent of proof-requiring compatibility, but it requires a conjecture to prove every true fact and no false one (too strong iff it implies a negative fact): the ILP mixture, not refutation of false data.
fix: Describe it as asking a conjecture to prove every true fact and no false one, the same mixture of the two compatibility notions as inductive logic programming (hedge 'as usually described' if content stays at secondary level).

label: related 'Probabilities on sentences'
problem: Sawin and Demski's result is stated without the coherence conditions under which the convergence property forces low probability on some short true Pi_2 sentences.
fix: 'show that computable distributions that satisfy natural coherence conditions and come to believe the true Pi_1 sentences must give some short true Pi_2 sentences arbitrarily low probability'.

label: sec:kepler:pool, paragraph 'The pool and the data'
problem: 'The eccentric circle of Hipparchus' for Mars is a misattribution: Hipparchus's eccentric is his solar model, and Ptolemy reports he did not construct planetary models (sources differ).
fix: 'the eccentric circle (the form of Hipparchus's solar theory)' or just 'the eccentric circle'.

label: abstract
problem: 'The classical reply to Hempel's theoretician's dilemma' is ambiguous: §8 distinguishes three replies with different verdicts.
fix: 'the classical reply that Craigian axiomatisations are unmanageable becomes a theorem about Craig's construction, not about theoretical vocabulary'.

label: Acknowledgements (last sentence)
problem: 'Hänni takes responsibility for the content of this paper' sits uneasily with the epistemic policy (the assessments are the authors' own and some depart from Hänni's notes), is absent from the companion papers, and is marked in the source as for the author to confirm.
fix: Ask the author; if unconfirmed, delete it or write 'Both authors are responsible for the content of this paper.'
